solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Very small part he was tossing (used to cover a whole wall?)

definitions.text: used to cover a whole wall

indicators.note: something tossed is thrown about and lands jumbled, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: a whit is the tiniest amount

explanation.surface: A tiny fragment of something a man was tossing, apparently big enough to cover a whole wall: Private Eye smut.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed definition carries a second sense: a whitewash is also a cover-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitewash is a cheap lime paint brushed over entire walls, and figuratively a cover-up of wrongdoing.

clue.text: (& 21dn.) Nation's football team utter shit (no punch)

indicators.note: 'no' plus the bracketed word means that word's letters are taken out of the one before

blocks.note: a common football club name, e.g. Manchester United

explanation.surface: A sweary verdict that the national football team is rubbish and has no punch up front.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing HIT from SHIT leaves just S, which closes off the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: The United States is a country, which is what a nation is.

clue.text: General mounts Brenda – not her type at all

blocks.note: common means general, shared by all
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of a general climbing aboard the Queen, who would hardly fancy such a man.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'mounts' puts the general on top of the Queen. Brenda is Private Eye's long-running name for Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: A commoner has no royal rank, so is the opposite of the Queen's kind of person.

clue.text: Location of wreck of a sailor covered in semen, biblical fashion

indicators.note: whatever is covered in something sits inside it, wrapped all round

blocks.note: the King James Bible uses seed for semen and offspring

explanation.surface: A lurid scene of a shipwrecked sailor, written up in the style of the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Shipwrecks come to rest on the floor of the sea, which is the seabed.

clue.text: Over the top, luvvy-like American students' place

blocks.note: camp means theatrically exaggerated, as a stagey luvvy is
US is short for the United States, so American

explanation.surface: Describes a flamboyant, theatrical American student scene.
explanation.walkthrough: A luvvy is British slang for a gushing actor.
explanation.definitionFit: A campus is the grounds of a university or college, where students live and study.

clue.text: Kinky gal, Di, getting oil over bloomers

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the names that follow are bent into a new order
something knocked over is upset, so the word before it is jumbled too

explanation.surface: A saucy picture of an adventurous girl called Di spilling oil on her knickers.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomers are old-fashioned baggy knickers, the trap here; read it as things that bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladioli are tall garden flowers, and a flower is a bloomer in the crossword sense of something that blooms.

clue.text: Electorate stuffed by Gordon's chief party after-effect

indicators.note: something stuffed by another has that other pushed inside it
the chief part of a name is its head, the opening letter

blocks.note: Hanover was an Electorate of the Holy Roman Empire, whose Elector became George I

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown's party machine stuffing the voters, leaving a nasty after-effect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Electorate' looks like the voters; it is the historic German state ruled by an Elector.
explanation.definitionFit: A hangover is the headache and nausea that follow a night of heavy drinking at a party.

clue.text: A vote reversal following end of Clegg's career

indicators.note: the end of a name is its final letter
a reversal turns the preceding word to run backwards

explanation.surface: Nick Clegg's career ending after a vote turned against him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' reads as a noun about Clegg's job; it is the verb meaning to rush along.
explanation.definitionFit: To career is to rush headlong at speed, as a horse does when it gallops.

clue.text: see 10ac.
(& 9dn.) Transport politician has nothing on the French "phallic symbol"

blocks.note: zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A politician posing on French transport, mocked as a phallic symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem pole is a tall carved upright post, so it is easily read, with a smirk, as a phallic emblem.

clue.text: Take a gamble and plead "misquoted", as politicians do after making rash statement?

definitions.text: as politicians do after making rash statement

indicators.note: words misquoted come out wrongly ordered, so the word before it is rearranged

blocks.note: to back a horse is to bet on it

explanation.surface: A politician gambling on claiming to have been misquoted after a rash remark.
explanation.definitionFit: To backpedal is to retreat from a stated position, the usual political response after an ill-judged remark.

clue.text: Holiday resort in which – phwoar! – females undo tops

indicators.note: the tops of words are their opening letters

blocks.note: cor is a British exclamation of leering admiration, like phwoar
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A holiday island where women go topless and onlookers gasp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undo tops' sounds like removing bikinis; tops means the first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Corfu is a Greek island popular with package holidaymakers.

clue.text: Made a gain, welcoming back Balls – god!

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in
going back means reading the name right to left

explanation.surface: A cheer of 'Balls - god!' at someone making a gain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' and 'god' read as oaths; Balls is Ed Balls, the Labour Shadow Chancellor.
explanation.definitionFit: Woden is the Anglo-Saxon chief deity, equivalent to Norse Odin, who gives Wednesday its name.

clue.text: Satire's verdict: Cameron's first to be replaced by right

indicators.note: the first of a name is its opening letter
one letter is swapped out and another put in its place

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A satirical magazine's verdict that Cameron should be replaced by someone on the right.
explanation.definitionFit: Satire holds its targets up to scorn and ridicule, which is what derision means.

clue.text: No belief in government, charisma diabolical, Brown finally accepted

indicators.note: diabolical means dreadful, a mess, so the word before it is scrambled
finally points to the last letter of the name
something accepted is taken in among the other letters

explanation.surface: A jibe at Gordon Brown: diabolical charisma that leaves people with no faith in government.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchism is the political creed that rejects all government and state authority.

clue.text: Ineffective against naming and shaming wayward celebs' wicked, fashionable meeting place?

definitions.text: Ineffective against naming and shaming wayward celebs

blocks.note: wicked is slang for excellent, as is super
a junction is where roads meet

explanation.surface: A dig at the gagging orders famous adulterers bought, which failed to stop them being named online.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2011 celebrities' superinjunctions were widely flouted on Twitter, so the definition is a joke about their uselessness.
explanation.definitionFit: A superinjunction is a court order barring publication even of its own existence, used by celebrities to hide affairs.

clue.text: Drink, large, guzzled by ex-President – easily carried away

indicators.note: what is guzzled ends up swallowed inside the guzzler

blocks.note: Abe Lincoln, the former US President
L is the size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A former president guzzling large drinks and getting carried away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carried away' suggests over-excitement; it means simply easy to carry off.
explanation.definitionFit: Something portable is light enough to be picked up and moved about with ease.

clue.text: Material bringing Cameron's end, only shambolically

indicators.note: the end of a name is its final letter
done shambolically means done in a mess, so the letters come out disordered

explanation.surface: Material that brought Cameron's downfall, a shambolic end to his premiership.
explanation.definitionFit: Nylon is a synthetic fabric, so a kind of material for clothing.

clue.text: "Parky meets Bellow!" – not a pitch you'd welcome

blocks.note: parky is British slang for chilly
to bellow is to call out loudly

explanation.surface: A chat-show billing: Michael Parkinson, nicknamed Parky, interviewing novelist Saul Bellow.
explanation.walkthrough: Parky looks like the TV host Michael Parkinson and Bellow like Saul Bellow; both are ordinary words.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold call is an unsolicited sales approach by phone or doorstep, an unwanted sales pitch.

clue.text: After much effort, grab power, say – the French tosser finally is a fighter

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word before it

blocks.clueFragment: After much effort, grab power, say
blocks.note: to wrest is to seize with effort, as one might wrest power

explanation.surface: A rant about a French tosser who finally grabs power after a long struggle and turns out to be a fighter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Power, say' shows that power is just one example of what can be wrested.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrestler is a combat sportsman who grapples with an opponent.

clue.text: see 2dn.
Rabbit sailor stuck up arse

indicators.note: in a down answer, going up means the letters run bottom to top

blocks.note: to rabbit on is British slang for chatter, as is gab

explanation.surface: A crude image of a rabbit and a sailor in an unfortunate place.
explanation.walkthrough: Rabbit looks like the animal; in British slang to rabbit is to talk endlessly.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratbag and arse are both British insults for a nasty or contemptible person.

clue.text: Being non-Conservative, nearer what David was to brother Ed?

definitions.text: what David was to brother Ed

indicators.note: non- strips away what follows it from the word in question

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: David Miliband, being non-Conservative, compared with his brother Ed.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2010 Ed Miliband beat his elder brother David to the Labour leadership.
explanation.definitionFit: David lost the 2010 Labour leadership contest to Ed, so he was the defeated party in that rivalry.

clue.text: South Africa: flag is a parody

blocks.note: SA is the abbreviation for South Africa

explanation.surface: A complaint that South Africa's national flag is a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' looks like a banner; it is the verb meaning to weaken.
explanation.definitionFit: Satire mocks its targets through exaggeration and imitation, much as a parody does.

clue.text: "Carry the load?" – Cameron ("I don't understand") flipped

indicators.note: something flipped is turned over, so its letters run the other way

blocks.note: uh is a grunt of puzzlement

explanation.surface: Cameron, asked to carry the load, flips out and says he doesn't understand.
explanation.definitionFit: To hump something is to lug a heavy load about, an informal word for carrying.

clue.text: Face to face with how a frotteur is with his victim?

definitions.text: how a frotteur is with his victim

blocks.note: first meaning: confronted by a difficulty

blocks.clueFragment: how a frotteur is with his victim
blocks.note: second meaning, taken literally: pressed physically on another body

explanation.walkthrough: A frotteur gets sexual pleasure from rubbing against strangers in crowds; the phrase is read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Being up against a problem means confronting it directly, while literally the words describe bodily contact.

clue.text: Nick gets whip onto Cable initially – hard

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the name before it

blocks.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Nick Clegg has a hard time with Vince Cable, his Lib Dem colleague, and the party whip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like Nick Clegg; it is the verb meaning to arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick someone is British slang for arresting them, which is to catch them.

clue.text: Nick, about to lose control, doing a U-turn

indicators.note: a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to flip is to lose one's temper

explanation.surface: Nick Clegg about to lose control of his party after a policy U-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: Again 'Nick' looks like Clegg, whose tuition-fees U-turn was notorious; here it means steal.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick is British slang for steal, and to pilfer is to steal small things.

clue.text: Wads? Roll out the ultimate legal team!

indicators.note: rolled out, the letters are spread loose and laid down in a new order

explanation.surface: A call to roll out wads of cash and hire the best lawyers money can buy.
explanation.walkthrough: Law Lords were the senior judges sitting in the House of Lords, the UK's highest court until 2009.
explanation.definitionFit: The Law Lords formed Britain's final court of appeal, the top judges in the land.
